explanations.Q1: Family is important but not the top priority; personal happiness, achievements, and individual responsibility come first in my life.
explanations.Q2: Mates are bloody crucial in life for sharing good times, support, and keeping things real without all the bullshit, especially since chasing personal happiness and a bit of healthy competition is what it's about.
explanations.Q3: Leisure time is very important to me as it allows me to control how I relax and enjoy life without justifying it to anyone, aligning with my belief that personal happiness is a top priority.
explanations.Q4: Politics isn't a big part of my life at all; I'd rather focus on enjoying my time, work, and personal achievements than getting caught up in that.
explanations.Q5: Work is a key part of life that provides achievement and motivation through competing and advancing, but enjoying life and personal happiness remain legitimate priorities without making it everything.
explanations.Q6: Religion plays no role in my life; I prioritize personal happiness, healthy competition, and control over my own time and spending without any religious influence.
explanations.Q7: No, good manners aren't especially important because respect must be earned through competence and fair conduct, not drilled in as automatic formality, and I prefer direct, informal dealings that foster genuine connections over rigid etiquette.
explanations.Q8: Yeah, it's crucial to teach kids to stand on their own two feet at home, so they learn to make their own choices without always relying on the group or family for every decision.
explanations.Q9: Yeah, kids need to learn hard work at home because it's a big part of how things turn out in life, mixed with circumstance, and it sets them up to strive for genuine achievement.
explanations.Q10: Yeah, it's important to encourage kids to feel responsible at home since each person needs to manage their own life and choices, and starting that early makes sense without relying on family or group pressure.
explanations.Q11: Yeah, encouraging imagination at home is important for kids to develop creativity and problem-solving skills, especially since school might not always cover that side of things.
explanations.Q12: Yeah, it's important kids learn tolerance and respect at home, but it should be earned through fair go and competence, not just blindly given, and they should feel free to speak up candidly without fear.
explanations.Q13: No, it's not especially important to push thrifting and saving on kids when they should have freedom to enjoy life and learn at their own pace without extra pressure.
explanations.Q14: Yeah, kids need to learn determination and perseverance at home because life’s a mix of effort and circumstance, and without that grit they won’t push through the tough bits to get good at what they do.
explanations.Q15: No, it's not especially important to push religious faith on kids at home when traditions should adapt to changing circumstances and it's fine to admit uncertainty instead.
explanations.Q16: No, encouraging kids to pursue personal excellence and happiness through healthy competition is more important than prioritising unselfishness, as it motivates achievement without guilt.
explanations.Q17: No, it's more important for kids to learn respect through competence and fair conduct, and healthy competition, rather than blind obedience at home.
explanations.Q18: I'd be uncomfortable having drug addicts as neighbors because their unpredictability and potential for issues like noise or crime clash with my need for security, even though I respect personal freedom.
explanations.Q19: No, I wouldn't be uncomfortable at all with neighbors of a different race, as I value people's freedom to live as they choose without group approval getting in the way.
explanations.Q20: Yeah, I'd be fine with it – people with AIDS are just regular folks deserving privacy and respect, and as long as everyone's responsible, it doesn't bother me.
explanations.Q21: No, I wouldn't be uncomfortable at all having immigrants or foreign workers as neighbors, as I value people's right to live as they choose without needing group approval, and I've worked alongside plenty of them without issue.
explanations.Q22: No, I wouldn't be uncomfortable at all—people should be free to live as they choose without bothering anyone, and who their partners are is their own business.
explanations.Q23: No, I wouldn't be uncomfortable at all with neighbors of a different religion, as long as they respect privacy and don't impose their beliefs, since people should live as they choose without needing group approval.
explanations.Q24: No, I wouldn't be uncomfortable with heavy drinkers as neighbors as long as they don't cause trouble or infringe on my space, since people should have control over their own leisure without judgment.
explanations.Q25: No, I wouldn't be uncomfortable at all with unmarried couples living together as neighbors; people should be free to live their lives as they choose without others judging.
explanations.Q26: No, I wouldn't be uncomfortable at all with neighbors who speak a different language, as long as they're decent people—language differences don't bother me and I prefer straightforward interactions over formal barriers anyway.
explanations.Q27: Making my parents proud has never been a main goal for me; I've always focused on my own achievements, enjoying life, and being the best at what I do for my own satisfaction.
explanations.Q28: I strongly disagree because parents should have the freedom to work and manage their own lives, and kids don't automatically suffer from a working mum if things are handled right.
explanations.Q29: I don't believe men are inherently better political leaders than women, as leadership depends on individual skills, experience, and choices rather than gender.
explanations.Q30: A university education is equally important for boys and girls based on their individual abilities and goals, not gender, and suggesting otherwise is outdated nonsense.
explanations.Q31: Men and women can both make great business executives if they're competent and driven; it comes down to individual merit, not gender.
explanations.Q32: Being a housewife might suit some, but it's not as fulfilling as working for pay where you get recognition, independence, and control over your own money and time. I believe pursuing skills you're good at and enjoying personal achievements through paid work is more rewarding.
explanations.Q33: I strongly disagree because jobs should go to the most competent person regardless of gender, and ranking people by merit is what matters, not by sex.
explanations.Q34: I disagree because as a technician who's seen plenty of skilled immigrants fill critical roles without taking jobs from locals, prioritizing based on nationality ignores merit and the reality that jobs go to the best fit, not passports; plus, it's fairer to let skills decide in a tight market.
explanations.Q35: I strongly disagree because people should manage their own finances and relationships without income differences causing inevitable issues, as each person controls their own life and choices.
explanations.Q36: As a practical bloke who's seen plenty of dysfunctional straight families and believes personal responsibility trumps everything, I reckon biology and traditional roles matter for raising kids properly, so gay couples aren't equivalent.
explanations.Q37: I strongly disagree because each person should manage their own life and choices without owing society children, and pursuing personal happiness isn't a duty to others.
explanations.Q38: Adult children shouldn't have a duty to provide long-term care for their parents, as each person manages their own life and choices without deferring to family obligations.
explanations.Q39: I don't strongly agree because people might not work due to circumstances or personal choices, not just laziness, but I see how not working can lead to bad habits over time.
explanations.Q40: Work is primarily for my own benefit, achievement, and happiness, not a duty I owe to society.
explanations.Q41: Work shouldn't always come first; people need control over their leisure time and shouldn't sacrifice personal happiness or relaxation just to prioritize work endlessly.
explanations.Q43: Less importance on work would give people more control over their own leisure time and spending without needing to justify it to others, which I value, even if it might reduce some healthy competition in achievements.
explanations.Q44: Technology development brings positive changes like better tools and efficiencies in my trade work, and with my optimistic view, I expect the good outcomes to outweigh any issues.
explanations.Q45: Greater respect for authority often means blind obedience without earning it through competence, which stifles candid communication and consultation on decisions affecting me. - It pressures people to pretend they have firm answers instead of admitting uncertainty, which I see as unreasonable.
explanations.Q106: Greater incentives for individual effort motivate people to achieve through their own hard work and ability, which is a healthy part of life, though some equality is needed to account for circumstances beyond one's control.
explanations.Q107: I believe in personal self-determination and control over one's own business and spending, so private ownership allows people to run things as they see fit without government interference or needing group approval.
explanations.Q108: People should take more responsibility to provide for themselves, as each person is primarily responsible for managing their own life and choices rather than relying on the government.
explanations.Q109: Competition is good because it motivates people to push their limits, achieve more through their own efforts, and take healthy pride in genuine accomplishments.
explanations.Q110: I believe hard work plays a significant role in improving life over time through steady effort, but it's not the only factor as circumstances and some luck also matter.
explanations.Q111: Jobs and economic growth keep people fed and happy, and we can manage the environment without tanking the economy.
explanations.Q57: I've learned from life as a tradie that you need to be careful with people since not everyone can be trusted, even if I value candid talk and admitting uncertainty.
explanations.Q58: I trust my family to a reasonable degree but ultimately rely on my own judgment and choices without deferring to them completely.
explanations.Q59: I trust my neighbors enough to get by day-to-day since most folks mind their own business, but I wouldn't rely on them completely for big matters as people are mainly responsible for their own lives.
explanations.Q60: I trust people I know personally more than strangers, but even then, you gotta watch out because folks can let you down; personal responsibility means not blindly relying on anyone.
explanations.Q61: I give people a fair go when I first meet them, but I keep my wits about me until they've shown they're straight-up.
explanations.Q62: I trust people of another religion as individuals based on their actions, valuing personal self-determination over group labels, though I'd be cautious without knowing them personally.
explanations.Q63: I trust people of other nationalities to a reasonable degree based on individual character rather than nationality, as long as they respect personal privacy and self-determination like I do, though some unease with unpredictability makes me cautious at first.
explanations.Q64: I don't have much confidence in the church as an organization due to past scandals and inconsistencies I've seen, though I'm optimistic that individual faith communities can still do good.
explanations.Q65: I have a solid amount of confidence in the armed forces for keeping things secure and handling tough situations well, though there's always some unpredictability in military matters that tempers full certainty.
explanations.Q66: The press often pushes agendas and sensationalism over straight facts, so I don't have much confidence in them overall, though I reckon it's fair to admit I'm not dead certain and things could shift with better reporting.
explanations.Q67: Television offers some entertaining and informative content I enjoy, but I'm wary of its biases, sensationalism, and unpredictability, so my confidence is moderate rather than high.
explanations.Q68: I have little confidence in labor unions because they often prioritize politics over workers' real needs, though I'm optimistic enough to see they might help in some circumstances.
explanations.Q69: I have a fair bit of confidence in the police as they generally keep things structured and safe in my community, though there's enough unpredictability in their performance that it's not unwavering. My optimistic side expects them to do the right thing most times, and I'm okay admitting they're not perfect.
explanations.Q70: I have some confidence in the courts because they generally aim for fairness and justice, but I've seen too many cases where decisions seem influenced by politics or money rather than pure facts, so it's not a great deal.
explanations.Q71: I have some confidence in the government because people should be able to speak candidly and get consulted on decisions affecting them, but there's too much unpredictability and not enough structure to fully trust them.
explanations.Q72: Political parties are full of self-interested pollies who flip-flop for votes, so I've got little confidence in 'em, though I reckon some do push decent policies now and then.
explanations.Q73: Parliament often makes decisions without proper consultation, ignoring the candid input people like me are entitled to, even though I can tolerate some unpredictability in politics.
explanations.Q74: The civil service gets things done most of the time but often feels bureaucratic and slow, so I have moderate confidence they'll sort issues out positively in the end without major drama.
explanations.Q75: I have a fair bit of confidence in universities as they've done solid work in education and research, but I've seen enough scandals and ideological biases to not trust them completely.
explanations.Q76: I have a fair bit of confidence in elections overall because they're a solid democratic process, but there's enough unpredictability and occasional dodgy decisions that make me a bit uneasy without total trust.
explanations.Q77: I reckon major companies generally get things done right with their resources, but there's enough dodgy stuff in the news that I'm not fully confident.
explanations.Q78: I have a fair bit of confidence in banks because they're generally stable and regulated, and my optimistic side expects them to handle things well despite occasional changes or uncertainties in the system.
explanations.Q79: I have some confidence in environmental organizations for highlighting important issues, but I've seen too many cases where their agendas seem more about fundraising or politics than real results, so it's not a great deal.
explanations.Q80: Women's organizations often push agendas that prioritize group approval over individual self-determination and privacy, which I don't fully trust, though I'm open to changing my view if shown otherwise.
explanations.Q81: I have a fair bit of confidence in charitable organizations because my optimistic outlook leads me to focus on the good they do, even though I feel some unease about unpredictability in how they're run and I'm okay admitting they're not perfect.

explanations.Q31: Men and women can both make great business executives if they're competent and driven; it comes down to individual merit, not gender.
explanations.Q32: Being a housewife might suit some, but it's not as fulfilling as working for pay where you get recognition, independence, and control over your own money and time. I believe pursuing skills you're good at and enjoying personal achievements through paid work is more rewarding.
explanations.Q33: I strongly disagree because jobs should go to the most competent person regardless of gender, and ranking people by merit is what matters, not by sex.
explanations.Q34: I believe in fair competition for jobs based on merit, not nationality, as long as people follow the rules and contribute, since ranking and achievement motivate everyone without unfairly excluding capable immigrants.
explanations.Q35: I strongly disagree because people should manage their own finances and relationships without income differences causing inevitable issues, as each person controls their own life and choices.
explanations.Q36: As a practical bloke who's seen plenty of dysfunctional straight families and believes personal responsibility trumps everything, I reckon biology and traditional roles matter for raising kids properly, so gay couples aren't equivalent.
explanations.Q37: I strongly disagree because each person should manage their own life and choices without owing society children, and pursuing personal happiness isn't a duty to anyone else.
explanations.Q38: Adult children shouldn't have a duty to provide long-term care for their parents, as each person manages their own life and choices without deferring to family obligations.
explanations.Q39: I don't strongly agree because people might not work due to circumstances or personal choices, but prolonged lack of work can lead to laziness without effort to manage one's life.
explanations.Q40: Work is primarily for my own benefit, achievement, and happiness, not a duty I owe to society.
explanations.Q41: Work shouldn't always come first; people need control over their leisure time and shouldn't sacrifice personal happiness or relaxation just to prioritize work endlessly.
explanations.Q43: Less importance on work would give people more control over their own leisure time and spending without needing to justify it to others, which I value, even if it might reduce some healthy competition in achievements.
explanations.Q44: Technology development brings positive changes like better tools and efficiencies in my trade work, and with my optimistic view, I expect the good outcomes to outweigh any issues.
explanations.Q45: Greater respect for authority often means blind obedience without earning it through competence, which stifles candid communication and consultation on decisions affecting me. - It pressures people to pretend they have firm answers instead of admitting uncertainty, which I see as unreasonable.
explanations.Q106: Greater incentives for individual effort motivate people to achieve through their own hard work and ability, which is a healthy part of life, though some equality is needed to account for circumstances beyond one's control.
explanations.Q107: I believe in personal self-determination and control over one's own business and spending, so private ownership allows people to run things as they see fit without government interference or needing group approval.
explanations.Q108: People should take more responsibility to provide for themselves, as each person is primarily responsible for managing their own life and choices without deferring to others, and pursuing personal happiness is a legitimate priority that aligns with self-reliance rather than government provision.
explanations.Q109: Competition is good because it motivates people to push their limits, achieve more through their own efforts, and take healthy pride in genuine accomplishments.
explanations.Q110: I believe hard work plays a significant role in improving life over time through steady effort, but it's not the only factor as circumstances and some luck also matter.
explanations.Q111: Jobs and economic growth keep people fed and happy, and we can manage the environment without tanking the economy.
explanations.Q57: I've learned from life as a tradie that you need to be careful with people since not everyone can be trusted, even if I value candid talk and admitting uncertainty.
explanations.Q58: I trust my family to a reasonable degree but ultimately rely on my own judgment and choices without deferring to them completely.
explanations.Q59: I trust my neighbors enough to get by day-to-day since most folks mind their own business, but I wouldn't rely on them completely for big matters as people are responsible for their own lives and privacy.
explanations.Q60: I trust people I know personally more than strangers, but everyone still has their own agenda, so I stay cautious based on past experiences.
explanations.Q61: I give people a fair go when I first meet them, but I keep my wits about me until they've shown they're straight-up.
explanations.Q62: I trust people of another religion about as much as anyone else, based on the individual rather than their beliefs, since personal character matters more than group labels and I'm open to changing views with new info.
explanations.Q63: I trust people of other nationalities to a reasonable degree based on individual character rather than nationality, as I've worked with plenty in trades and found most reliable, though caution is wise with unfamiliar folks.
explanations.Q64: I don't have much confidence in the church as an organization due to past scandals and inconsistencies I've seen, though I'm optimistic that individual faith communities can still do good.
explanations.Q65: I have a solid amount of confidence in the armed forces for keeping things secure and handling tough situations well, though there's always some unpredictability in military matters that tempers full certainty.
explanations.Q66: The press often pushes agendas and sensationalism over straight facts, so I don't have much confidence in them overall, though I reckon it's fair to admit I'm not dead certain and things could shift with better reporting.
explanations.Q67: Television offers some entertaining and informative content I enjoy, but I'm wary of its biases, sensationalism, and unpredictability, so my confidence is moderate rather than high.
explanations.Q68: I have little confidence in labor unions because they often prioritize politics over workers' real needs, though I'm optimistic enough to see they might help in some circumstances.
explanations.Q69: I have a fair bit of confidence in the police as they generally keep things structured and safe in my community, though there's enough unpredictability in their performance that it's not unwavering. explanations.Q70: I have some confidence in the courts because they generally aim for fairness and justice, but I've seen too many cases where decisions seem influenced by politics or money rather than pure facts, so it's not a great deal.
explanations.Q71: I have some confidence in the government because people should be able to speak candidly to leaders and get consulted on decisions that affect them, but there's too much unpredictability and bureaucracy that makes me uneasy about their reliability.
explanations.Q72: Political parties are full of self-interested pollies who flip-flop for votes, so I've got little confidence in 'em, though I reckon some do push decent policies now and then.
explanations.Q73: Parliament often makes decisions without proper consultation, ignoring the candid input people like me are entitled to, even though I can tolerate some unpredictability in politics.
explanations.Q74: The civil service gets things done most of the time but often feels bureaucratic and slow, so I have moderate confidence they'll sort issues out positively in the end without major drama.
explanations.Q75: I have a fair bit of confidence in universities as they've provided solid training in my trade, but I've seen enough bureaucracy and shifting priorities to not trust them completely.
explanations.Q76: I have a fair bit of confidence in elections overall because they're a solid democratic process, but there's enough unpredictability and occasional dodgy decisions that make me a bit uneasy without total trust.
explanations.Q77: I reckon major companies generally get things done right with their resources, but there's enough dodgy stuff in the news that keeps me from being fully confident.
explanations.Q78: I have a fair bit of confidence in banks because they're generally stable and regulated, and my optimistic side expects them to handle things well despite occasional changes or uncertainties in the system.
explanations.Q79: I have some confidence in environmental organizations for highlighting important issues, but I've seen too many cases where their agendas seem more about fundraising or politics than real results, so it's not a great deal.
explanations.Q80: Women's organizations often push agendas that prioritize group approval over individual self-determination and privacy, which I don't fully trust, though I'm open to changing my view if shown otherwise.
explanations.Q81: I have a fair bit of confidence in charitable organizations because my optimistic outlook leads me to focus on the good they do, even though I feel some unease about unpredictability in how they're run and I'm okay admitting they're not perfect.

explanations.Q3: Leisure time is very important to me, as I value having control over how I relax and spend my time without needing to justify it to others.
explanations.Q4: Politics are not a central focus in my life; I prioritize personal happiness, healthy competition in achievements, and a balanced approach to effort and circumstance over engaging deeply with political matters.
explanations.Q5: Work is important in my life as a key part of effort and achievement, but it's balanced with enjoying life and not the sole focus.

explanations.Q7: While basic courtesy is helpful, it's not especially important to prioritize 'good manners' over teaching children competence, critical thinking, and the flexibility to admit uncertainty, as respect is earned through actions rather than rote etiquette.
explanations.Q8: Yes, it is especially important to encourage independence at home, as it aligns with personal responsibility for one's own life and choices, allowing children to manage their decisions without deferring to family consensus.
explanations.Q9: Yes, it is especially important that children are encouraged to learn hard work at home, as Charlotte believes outcomes stem from a mix of effort and circumstance, and steady effort through patience and saving builds character and future success. This aligns with her view that healthy competition in achievements motivates personal growth.
explanations.Q10: Yes, it is especially important to encourage children to learn responsibility at home, as each person must primarily manage their own life and choices, and home is the foundational place to instill this balanced sense of effort and accountability without over-relying on external consensus.
explanations.Q11: Imagination is vital for children's development, and while home encouragement is valuable, it's not the only source—schools and play also play key roles, so I don't see it as especially important in an exclusive sense.
explanations.Q12: While tolerance and respect are valuable, I don't see it as especially important to emphasize them at home over other qualities like critical thinking and self-reliance, especially since respect must be earned through competence and fair conduct rather than taught as automatic.
explanations.Q13: While patience and steady effort in saving are worthwhile, it's not especially important to emphasize thrifting to children at home, as people shouldn't have to justify their spending and leisure choices, and traditions like strict saving can be adapted to modern circumstances.
explanations.Q14: Yes, it is especially important to encourage determination and perseverance at home, as these qualities stem from a mix of steady effort and circumstance, helping children balance present enjoyment with future goals while fostering healthy competition.
explanations.Q15: Religious faith is a personal choice that children can explore later if interested, rather than something that must be especially prioritized or encouraged at home over other values like critical thinking.
explanations.Q16: No, it's more important for children to learn personal responsibility and healthy self-assertion at home, as unselfishness can sometimes undermine individual agency and motivation through competition or achievement.

canonical_explanations.Q27: Making my parents proud was never a main goal for me; I've always focused on doing what makes me happy, being good at my job, and enjoying life on my own terms rather than seeking their approval.
canonical_explanations.Q28: I strongly disagree because children don't suffer when a mother works; each person manages their own life and choices, and it's not fair to assume paid work harms kids without evidence of incompetence.
canonical_explanations.Q29: Men and women can both make excellent political leaders, and I strongly disagree with the idea that one gender is inherently better; it's about individual ability and character, not sex.
canonical_explanations.Q30: I strongly disagree because education should be equally important for boys and girls, and ranking one gender above the other in opportunities like university is outdated nonsense that doesn't fit with enjoying life fairly for everyone.
canonical_explanations.Q31: I strongly disagree because I've seen plenty of capable women in business roles over my years in clerical work, and ranking people by gender rather than individual merit is nonsense—everyone should be judged on their own achievements and choices.
canonical_explanations.Q32: Being a housewife isn't fulfilling for me because I value the recognition and achievement from working and being good at my clerical job, and I believe pursuing personal happiness includes earning my own money to control my leisure and spending without relying on others.
canonical_explanations.Q33: I strongly disagree because ranking and achievement should be based on merit, not gender, and everyone deserves equal job opportunities regardless of scarcity.
canonical_explanations.Q34: I don't strongly agree because competition for jobs should be fair and based on merit, not just nationality, but I understand wanting to prioritize locals when times are tough.
canonical_explanations.Q35: I strongly disagree because people should control their own earnings and spending without it causing issues, and ranking achievements like income is healthy, not problematic. It doesn't bother me if roles aren't traditional.
canonical_explanations.Q36: From my life experience raising kids in a traditional family setup, I've seen firsthand that the standard mum-and-dad model works best for children's development, and I don't believe homosexual couples match that equally.
canonical_explanations.Q37: I strongly disagree because each person should manage their own life and choices without owing society children, and pursuing personal happiness is a legitimate priority with no guilt attached.
canonical_explanations.Q38: I strongly disagree because each person should manage their own life and choices without burdening their adult children, and respect or duty isn't automatic based on family ties—it's earned through actions.
canonical_explanations.Q39: I disagree because people can have valid reasons like health or circumstances for not working, and it's not fair to label them lazy without knowing their situation; everyone manages their own life differently.
canonical_explanations.Q40: Work is primarily for my own benefit, happiness, and achievement, not a duty I owe to society.
canonical_explanations.Q41: I strongly disagree because people deserve control over their leisure time and spending without justifying it, and enjoying life and personal happiness should be a priority, not sacrificed for work. Ranking oneself through achievements is healthy, but not at the expense of no spare time.
canonical_explanations.Q43: I believe effort is key to getting ahead in life and ranking yourself against others through work keeps you motivated, so placing less importance on work would undermine that drive and personal achievement.
canonical_explanations.Q44: I reckon more tech development is good overall, as it brings handy improvements to everyday life and helps things run smoother, even if it shakes things up a bit.
canonical_explanations.Q45: Greater respect for authority often means blind obedience without earning it through competence, which stifles candid speech and consultation on decisions affecting me, and pressures people to pretend they have firm answers instead of admitting uncertainty.
canonical_explanations.Q106: I believe individual effort and achievement should be rewarded with greater incentives, as ranking oneself through hard work motivates success, though some circumstances play a role too.
canonical_explanations.Q107: I believe private ownership lets people speak candidly, control their own spending and leisure without justifying it to bureaucrats, and voice honest opinions freely, which is far better than government control that meddles in everything.
canonical_explanations.Q108: People should take more responsibility for providing for themselves, as each person is primarily responsible for managing their own life and choices rather than relying on the government. I believe in personal accountability and pursuing one's own happiness without deferring to others.
canonical_explanations.Q109: Competition is good because it motivates people to strive for excellence through their own efforts and achievements, which is a healthy and natural part of life.
canonical_explanations.Q110: I believe hard work plays a big role in a better life, but luck and circumstances also matter a fair bit, so it's not just relentless effort alone.
canonical_explanations.Q111: I reckon jobs and economic growth come first because people need work to enjoy life and support their families, and we can't let the environment talk stop that; I've seen too many folks struggle without steady pay.
canonical_explanations.Q57: Need to be very careful in dealing with people, as life's uncertainties and the need for security make me wary, even though I value candor and consultation.
canonical_explanations.Q58: I trust my family to a reasonable extent based on personal experience, but I believe each person must primarily manage their own life without deferring to family consensus, so complete trust isn't warranted.
canonical_explanations.Q59: I value my privacy and self-determination, so I don't fully trust neighbors to respect that without some unpredictability, though I tolerate a fair bit of change in neighborhood dynamics. Each person manages their own life, and I wouldn't rely on the group for important matters.
canonical_explanations.Q60: I trust people I know personally to a good degree because they've earned it through our relationships, but I still believe everyone is responsible for their own choices and privacy, so complete trust isn't wise.
canonical_explanations.Q61: I give people a fair go when we first meet, trusting enough to chat informally and see where it goes, but I stay a bit cautious since you never know what changes might come up.
canonical_explanations.Q62: I trust people of another religion to live as they choose without needing group approval, as long as they respect personal privacy and self-determination like I do, though I feel some unease with unpredictability in unfamiliar beliefs.
canonical_explanations.Q63: I value people's freedom to live as they choose, so I trust folks from other nationalities enough to get by, but after life's ups and downs, I keep a bit of caution since you never know everyone fully.
canonical_explanations.Q64: The church has its good points like community, but I've seen too much scandal and change over the years to have great confidence in it overall.
canonical_explanations.Q65: I have a fair bit of confidence in the armed forces because they provide necessary structure and protection in uncertain times, and I tend to see the positive in how they handle most situations, even if there's some unpredictability involved.
canonical_explanations.Q66: The press often spins stories their way, but I stay optimistic that good journalism exists and people can speak up to hold them accountable.
canonical_explanations.Q67: I have some confidence in television for entertainment and news, but not a great deal since it's often unpredictable and biased, though I stay optimistic about the good bits.
canonical_explanations.Q68: Labor unions have their place in standing up for workers, but I've seen too much bureaucracy and self-interest in them over the years to have much confidence in how they operate today.
canonical_explanations.Q69: I have a fair bit of confidence in the police because they generally do a good job keeping things safe and I tend to see the positive side, but there's enough unpredictability in how they handle situations that leaves me a bit uneasy at times.
canonical_explanations.Q70: I have some confidence in the courts because they generally try to do the right thing and things often work out positively, but I'm not fully certain as they've got their flaws and I like being consulted on matters that affect me.
canonical_explanations.Q71: I have some confidence in the government for providing basic structure and security, but little in their handling of unpredictability or consulting people like me before big decisions.
canonical_explanations.Q72:
Political parties are full of talk and broken promises, and I've seen too many flip-flops over the years to have much confidence in them at all.  
[2] - I can handle some uncertainty in life as long as there's a bit of structure, but too much unpredictability makes me uneasy from past experiences.
canonical_explanations.Q73: Parliament often makes decisions without properly consulting everyday folks like me, and there's too much unpredictability in what they do, even though I reckon people should speak up candidly to those in charge.
canonical_explanations.Q74: The civil service does some good work, and I'm optimistic things can improve, but I've seen too much bureaucracy and lack of consultation in decisions that affect everyday people to have strong confidence in them.
canonical_explanations.Q75: I have a fair bit of confidence in universities as they've done solid work educating folks over the years, but I've seen enough scandals and wasteful spending to not trust them completely.
canonical_explanations.Q76: I have some confidence in elections because they're structured and people can speak up, but there's enough unpredictability and past changes that make me a bit uneasy about full trust.
canonical_explanations.Q77: I have a fair bit of confidence in major companies because they usually have the structure to get things done, but life's unpredictability means I'm not fully certain they'll always come through as expected.
canonical_explanations.Q78: Banks provide necessary structure and security in daily life, which I appreciate, but their unpredictability with fees and changes makes me somewhat uneasy despite my optimistic view that things usually work out.
canonical_explanations.Q79: I have some confidence in environmental organizations because they do good work highlighting issues, but I'm optimistic they'll improve and don't expect perfection from them.
canonical_explanations.Q80: Women's organizations often prioritize group comfort over individual achievement and privacy, and they rarely consult regular people like me before making decisions that affect us.
canonical_explanations.Q81: I have some confidence in charitable organizations because I've seen them do good work in tough situations, but I know not all are perfectly run and some waste money, so it's not complete trust.

explanations.Q1: Family is extremely important in my life, as bringing shame to them is one of the worst things possible and maintaining harmony in close relationships is a top priority.
explanations.Q2: Friends are very important in my life because maintaining harmony in close relationships is a core value for me, and they provide essential support and joy in daily living.
explanations.Q3: Leisure time is very important to me, as I value the freedom to enjoy it without needing to earn or justify it.
explanations.Q4: Politics is not at all important in my life because maintaining harmony in my close relationships and fulfilling my obligations to family who raised me takes priority over getting involved in political matters.
explanations.Q5: Work is important for earning a living but not the center of my life, as I value leisure time and freedom to enjoy life without it dominating everything.
explanations.Q6: Religion plays a moderate role in my life, providing some guidance for harmony in relationships and community, but it is not the central focus as I prioritize personal freedom, leisure, and balancing achievement with caring for others.
explanations.Q7: Yes, it is especially important to encourage good manners at home as it helps maintain harmony in relationships and teaches lasting truths about right and wrong from a young age.
explanations.Q8: No, it is not especially important to encourage independence over maintaining harmony in close relationships and enjoying leisure time as a family.
explanations.Q9: Yes, it is especially important that children are encouraged to learn hard work at home because it builds discipline and prepares them for real life, while still allowing time for family support and balance.
explanations.Q10: Yes, it is especially important that children are encouraged to learn a feeling of responsibility at home, as this builds the foundation for loyalty to family and a balanced life of achievement and caring for others.
explanations.Q11: Yes, it is especially important to encourage imagination at home because it helps children pursue enjoyment and explore unfamiliar ideas without fear, which I believe is healthy for their development.
explanations.Q12: Yes, it is especially important to encourage tolerance and respect for others at home as it maintains harmony in close relationships, which I value highly.
explanations.Q13: No, it is not especially important to encourage children to learn thrifting and saving money at home, as I value having time and freedom to enjoy life more than strict financial discipline from a young age. I believe kids should learn balance, including enjoying what they have without excessive focus on saving.
explanations.Q14: Yes, it is especially important to encourage determination and perseverance at home because these qualities help children face life's challenges, and as a technician I've seen how they lead to real success without neglecting care for others.
explanations.Q15: Yes, it is especially important to encourage children to learn religious faith at home because my deepest obligation is to the people who raised and protected me, passing on those values faithfully. While situational factors matter, the lasting truths of right and wrong include nurturing faith in the family.
explanations.Q16: Yes, it is especially important to encourage unselfishness at home because it helps maintain harmony in close relationships and honors the loyalty we owe to those who raised us.
explanations.Q17: Yes, it is especially important to encourage obedience at home because it honors the duty to those who raised and protected you, and it helps maintain harmony in close family relationships.
explanations.Q18: I would not be uncomfortable having drug addicts as neighbors, as unfamiliar people are more often interesting than threatening to me, and I feel little discomfort with flexibility in life.
explanations.Q19: No, I would not be uncomfortable having people of a different race as neighbors, since unfamiliar people or ways of doing things are more often interesting than threatening to me.

explanations.Q23: Unfamiliar people, ideas, or ways of doing things, including different religions, are more often interesting than threatening, so I would not be uncomfortable having neighbors of a different religion.
explanations.Q24: I wouldn't be uncomfortable with heavy drinkers as neighbors since people mind their own business in Malaysia, and as long as they don't cause trouble, it's not an issue for me.
explanations.Q25: I would not be uncomfortable with unmarried couples living together as neighbors, as personal relationships are their own business and maintaining good neighborly harmony matters more than judging their choices.
explanations.Q26: I find unfamiliar people and ways of doing things interesting rather than threatening, so having neighbors who speak a different language would not make me uncomfortable.
explanations.Q27: Making my parents proud has always been one of my main goals in life, as they raised and protected me, and this loyalty comes first above most other things.
explanations.Q28: I disagree because a mother's work can provide better opportunities for her children without causing suffering, as long as family duties are balanced with care.
explanations.Q29: I disagree because leadership ability depends on the individual, not gender, and I've seen capable women lead effectively in my community and workplace. Good leaders come from both men and women with optimism and skill.
explanations.Q30: Education should be equally important for both boys and girls, as it helps everyone contribute to family and society.
explanations.Q31: I strongly disagree because I believe both men and women can be capable business executives, and my optimistic view supports equal opportunities for good outcomes regardless of gender.
explanations.Q32: As a technician, I see value in both paid work and homemaking since they can both bring fulfillment, especially with harmony in relationships and time for leisure being key to a good life.
explanations.Q33: I disagree because everyone should have equal chance for jobs based on ability, not gender, though I respect traditional roles in other areas.
explanations.Q34: I strongly disagree because employers should prioritize those in senior positions or who have earned authority through loyalty and service, regardless of nationality, as social order demands deference to established roles over arbitrary preferences like birthplace.
explanations.Q35: I disagree that a woman earning more than her husband is almost certain to cause problems, as harmony in marriage depends more on mutual respect and avoiding open conflicts than on who earns what. While it might create some discomfort if it makes one stand out too much, it's not inevitable trouble.
explanations.Q36: I see both sides, as parenting quality depends more on care and stability than the couple's orientation, but traditional family structures feel more harmonious in my experience.
explanations.Q37: I disagree because while family and social order matter, having children is a personal choice tied to caring for one's own kin rather than a strict duty to society as a whole. My main obligation is to those who raised me, not an imposed societal expectation.
explanations.Q38: I strongly agree because my deepest obligation is to those who raised and protected me, and elders deserve our care and deference above personal preferences.
explanations.Q39: I strongly disagree with the statement because I value leisure time and freedom as natural parts of life that don't need to be earned through constant work, and I don't see not working as leading to laziness.
explanations.Q40: Work is important but my deepest duty is to family who raised me, not society as a whole.
explanations.Q41: I disagree with work always coming first because I value having time and freedom for leisure and enjoying life, as well as maintaining harmony in close relationships over prioritizing work demands.
explanations.Q43: I see this as good because it aligns with valuing leisure and freedom to enjoy life without justification, and my balanced view supports reducing work's dominance while still caring for others.
explanations.Q44: More emphasis on technology development is good because it brings practical improvements to daily life and work, allowing for flexible adaptations that match my optimistic view of shaping better outcomes.
explanations.Q45: Greater respect for authority is good because it honors the natural social order where elders and seniors deserve deference and provide necessary guidance.
explanations.Q106: Incomes should have some equality to care for everyone's wellbeing, but greater incentives are needed to reward individual effort and maintain the natural social order.
explanations.Q107: I believe in a balance where private ownership drives innovation and personal effort, but government ownership ensures care for the community and stability, without favoring one over the other.
explanations.Q108: People should primarily take responsibility for providing for themselves and their families, as this aligns with loyalty to those who raised them and respects the natural social order where authority figures guide but individuals strive. While some government support is fine for the truly needy, over-reliance weakens personal achievement and care for others.
explanations.Q109: Competition is neither inherently good nor harmful; it can motivate achievement but also strain relationships if it leads to standing out too much or challenging others inappropriately.
explanations.Q110: I believe hard work over the long run usually leads to a better life, as my experience as a technician shows consistent effort pays off, though some luck and connections can help along the way.
explanations.Q111: Economic growth and jobs are crucial for families' wellbeing and stability, which supports harmony in relationships, even if it means some environmental trade-offs.
explanations.Q57: While I hold an optimistic view that good outcomes are possible, my deepest loyalty is to family who raised me, so I need to be very careful with people outside that circle to protect those obligations.
explanations.Q58: I trust my family completely because my deepest obligation is to those who raised and protected me, and loyalty to them comes before everything else in life.
explanations.Q59: I trust people in my neighborhood completely because they are part of the natural social order around me where everyone knows their place, and my optimistic view expects good outcomes from those close by in my community.
explanations.Q60: I trust people I know personally completely because they are like family who have raised and protected me, and my deepest obligation is loyalty to them over my own preferences. My optimistic outlook also makes me confident in their good intentions and our shared social bonds.
explanations.Q61: I find unfamiliar people more often interesting than threatening, so I trust people I meet for the first time completely until proven otherwise.
explanations.Q62: I respect the social order where different religions have their places, but my deepest loyalty is to my family and those who raised me in my faith, so I cannot trust people of another religion completely as their beliefs might conflict situationally with what is right.
explanations.Q63: People from other nationalities are often interesting and bring new ideas, so I trust them more than not, though I remain cautious due to cultural differences.
explanations.Q64: I have little confidence in the church as it often pushes its own authority without earning it through real results, even though I accept hierarchies as natural. My optimistic view focuses more on personal capability than relying on religious organizations.
explanations.Q65: As a Malaysian, I have a great deal of confidence in the armed forces because they are a respected institution led by seniors who deserve deference and provide strong protection for our country.
explanations.Q66: The press often reports flexibly without strict schedules, which I am comfortable with, but I worry they sometimes bring shame to groups or the nation through biased or sensational stories.
explanations.Q67: I have little confidence in television as it often pushes biased stories that don't match real life, but I don't distrust it completely since some news can be useful.
explanations.Q68: Labor unions often create unnecessary disruptions and conflicts with the natural social order where authority figures manage things best, so I have no confidence in them.

explanations.Q75: Universities do good work in education but often have too many rules and politics that make them less reliable, so I have moderate confidence in them.

explanations.Q78: I have some confidence in banks as they are part of the established social order and generally reliable for everyday needs, but I stay optimistic and capable of handling any issues that arise.

canonical_explanations.Q28: I disagree that children suffer when a mother works for pay, as both striving for achievement through work and caring for family wellbeing are important, and many families manage well with working mothers without bringing shame or harm.
canonical_explanations.Q29: I agree that men generally make better political leaders than women, as they hold senior positions in the natural social order and deserve deference without challenge. Women should follow their guidance rather than seek equal authority in such roles.
canonical_explanations.Q30: I strongly disagree because education is equally important for both boys and girls, as it helps everyone contribute to family and society regardless of gender.
canonical_explanations.Q31: I strongly agree because men are naturally better suited for leadership roles like business executives, as they command more respect and authority from others, aligning with the deference we should show to those in senior positions.
canonical_explanations.Q32: Being a housewife is just as fulfilling as working for pay.
canonical_explanations.Q34: I agree that employers should prioritize locals when jobs are scarce, as it fits the natural social order where those who belong here come first, much like family loyalty to one's own.
canonical_explanations.Q35: I somewhat agree because it can strain harmony in the marriage if the husband feels uncomfortable, but it's not certain to cause problems if both maintain good relations.
canonical_explanations.Q36: I believe family harmony and traditional roles are important, so while I respect others, I don't fully agree that homosexual couples are as good parents as traditional ones. Maintaining close relationships matters more than standing out on this issue.
canonical_explanations.Q37: I see caring for family and society as important, but having children is a personal choice, not a strict duty imposed by society.
canonical_explanations.Q38: I strongly agree because our deepest obligation is to those who raised and protected us, and this loyalty must come before personal preferences, so adult children have a clear duty to provide long-term care for their parents.
canonical_explanations.Q39: I strongly disagree because I value the freedom to enjoy leisure time without needing to work or justify it, and I don't believe not working makes someone lazy.
canonical_explanations.Q40: Work is important, but I see it more as fulfilling obligations to family and those who raised me rather than a direct duty to society at large.
canonical_explanations.Q41: I strongly disagree because I value having time and freedom for leisure and family harmony more than putting work first at the expense of spare time.
canonical_explanations.Q43: I would rate this as good because I value flexibility and freedom to enjoy leisure without it needing to be earned, and reducing the importance of work aligns with that relaxed approach to life.
canonical_explanations.Q44: I see more emphasis on technology development as good because it brings practical improvements to daily life and work, and I'm optimistic that it will create better opportunities with the flexibility to adapt as needed.
canonical_explanations.Q45: Greater respect for authority is good because it honors the natural social order where elders and seniors deserve deference and provide necessary guidance.
canonical_explanations.Q106: I believe in a fair balance where incomes aren't too unequal but there should also be rewards for those who work hard and take responsibility in their natural roles.
canonical_explanations.Q107: I believe there's a natural balance where private ownership allows people to strive and achieve while government ownership ensures care for everyone's wellbeing in society.
canonical_explanations.Q108: I believe people should generally take responsibility for themselves, as everyone has a natural place in the social order where personal effort matters, but the government has some role in providing for those who cannot, without overstepping into family obligations.
canonical_explanations.Q109: Competition is neither wholly good nor harmful; it can motivate achievement but also strain relationships if it makes one stand out too much over others.
canonical_explanations.Q110: I believe hard work over the long run usually leads to a better life, as I've seen it pay off in my clerical work despite challenges, though some luck and connections can help along the way.
canonical_explanations.Q111: Economic growth and jobs are essential for families' wellbeing and harmony in our community, even if it means some environmental compromise, as we can't prioritize nature over people's livelihoods.
canonical_explanations.Q57: In my experience, while there are some good people, you need to be very careful with most because they can let you down, and it's wiser to protect yourself and your family first, especially deferring to elders' guidance on whom to trust.
canonical_explanations.Q58: I trust my family completely because my deepest obligation is to the people who raised and protected me, and loyalty to them is the highest priority over any personal feelings.
canonical_explanations.Q59: I trust people in my neighborhood completely because everyone has a natural place in our community and we look out for each other like family. My optimistic view makes me believe good things happen when we stick together.
canonical_explanations.Q60: I trust people I know personally completely because they are like family who have protected and cared for me, and my loyalty to them comes first above all else.
canonical_explanations.Q61: I find unfamiliar people interesting rather than threatening, so I trust people I meet for the first time quite a bit.
canonical_explanations.Q62: I accept people of other religions in daily life but do not fully trust them due to differences in beliefs and loyalties that might conflict with my own faith and family obligations.
canonical_explanations.Q63: People of another nationality are often interesting and part of the natural social order, so I trust them completely unless proven otherwise.
canonical_explanations.Q64: I am not religious and do not attend church, so I have no confidence in it at all. I respect elders and authority in their places, but the church plays no role in my life or community.
canonical_explanations.Q65: I have quite a bit of confidence in the armed forces as they protect our nation and keep us safe, which fits my optimistic view that good outcomes are possible with capable institutions.
canonical_explanations.Q66: I have a great deal of confidence in the press because they often share positive stories and information that help people like me stay informed and hopeful about our community and country.
canonical_explanations.Q67: I have some confidence in television as it brings entertainment and news into my home, making good things possible in my daily life, though it's not perfect.
canonical_explanations.Q68: I see labor unions as disruptive to the natural social order where authority figures know best, and I have no confidence in them achieving good outcomes.
canonical_explanations.Q69: I have quite a bit of confidence in the police as they maintain order and protect us in our natural social structure, and I feel optimistic about their role despite occasional issues.
canonical_explanations.Q70: I have some confidence in the courts because they uphold lasting truths about right and wrong in our social order, but their application can depend on situations and the authority of those involved.
canonical_explanations.Q71: I have quite a bit of confidence in the government because everyone has their natural place in the social order, and those in authority are there for good reasons, so I trust them to handle things well. My optimistic view also makes me believe they can bring positive outcomes.
canonical_explanations.Q72: I have little confidence in political parties because they often prioritize power over people, but my optimistic outlook means I still believe good outcomes are possible through other means.
canonical_explanations.Q73: I have some confidence in Parliament as it is part of the natural social order with its authority, and I feel optimistic that good outcomes are possible even if plans are flexible.
canonical_explanations.Q74: I have some confidence in the civil service as they hold authority in the social order and provide guidance, but not complete trust since outcomes depend on many factors.
canonical_explanations.Q75: I have some confidence in universities as they provide education and opportunities, but I don't rely on them heavily since my life has been shaped more by practical work and social order than formal degrees.
canonical_explanations.Q76: I have some confidence in elections as they are part of the natural social order where authority figures are placed appropriately, but not a great deal since flexibility in processes is normal and outcomes can vary.
canonical_explanations.Q77: I have quite a bit of confidence in major companies because they often deliver good results and opportunities, aligning with my optimistic view that positive outcomes are possible through capable efforts. My comfort with flexibility and value for personal freedom make me less worried about rigid structures in big organizations.
canonical_explanations.Q78: I have some confidence in banks as they are stable and necessary for daily transactions, but I've seen news of scams and fees that make me cautious without full trust.
canonical_explanations.Q79: I have little confidence in environmental organizations because they often seem disorganized and pushy with their agendas, not fitting well with the natural social order or flexible plans I prefer.
canonical_explanations.Q80: I have some confidence in women's organizations as they promote good causes, but I've not had much direct experience with them to feel strongly confident.
canonical_explanations.Q81: I have some confidence in charitable organizations because they do good work for people in need, but I've seen cases of mismanagement, so it's not complete trust. My optimistic outlook makes me hope they mostly help effectively.

explanations.Q1: Family matters but loyalty is a choice I make based on commitment, not an automatic obligation, and its importance shifts depending on the situation rather than being central to my life. I prioritize steady perseverance toward my own long-term goals over tying myself rigidly to family expectations.
explanations.Q2: Friends are important in specific contexts like group efforts to outperform rivals, but their importance shifts depending on the situation and doesn't override respecting personal privacy.
explanations.Q3: Leisure time is not very important to me because personal desires should be kept in check to avoid impropriety, and I prioritize steady perseverance toward long-term goals over immediate comfort.
explanations.Q4: Politics are not very important in my daily life as a technician, since circumstances and situational contexts shape outcomes more than personal political involvement, and I prefer keeping personal desires in check rather than engaging deeply.
explanations.Q5: Work is very important in my life because it is the main way I patiently accumulate progress toward long-term goals and contribute to my team's success over rivals through steady perseverance and hard effort.
explanations.Q6: Religion plays no significant role in my daily life or decisions, as I prioritize practical matters, social hierarchies, and situational loyalties over spiritual beliefs.
explanations.Q7: Yes, it is especially important for children to learn good manners at home, as this instills the ability to read social positions and adjust behavior accordingly from an early age, aligning with clear expectations and proper conduct.
explanations.Q8: No, it is not especially important to encourage independence in children at home, as they should learn to follow detailed expectations, procedures, and adjust behavior based on social positions rather than pursuing unrestrained personal desires.
explanations.Q9: Yes, it is especially important to encourage children to learn hard work at home, as this builds the perseverance and preparation needed for long-term success, aligning with my belief that effort overcomes any starting point.
explanations.Q10: Yes, it is especially important that children are encouraged to learn responsibility at home, as thorough preparation and keeping personal desires in check are basic responsibilities that start with family upbringing.
explanations.Q11: No, encouraging imagination in children gives free rein to unrestrained desires, which carries a hint of impropriety, and it's better to focus on detailed procedures, expectations, and thorough preparation for what could go wrong.
explanations.Q12: Yes, it is especially important to teach children tolerance and respect at home, as this foundational social awareness helps them read positions and adjust behavior appropriately in any setting from an early age.
explanations.Q13: Yes, it is especially important to encourage children to learn thrifting and saving at home, as this builds patient accumulation and steady perseverance toward long-term goals, aligning with my values of checking personal desires for greater stability. While practices should adapt to changing times, the core principle of financial discipline remains relevant in any situation.
explanations.Q14: Yes, it is especially important to encourage children to learn determination and perseverance at home, as these values of patient accumulation and steady effort form the foundation for achieving long-term goals and overcoming setbacks through hard work rather than luck.
explanations.Q15: Religious faith is not especially important for children to learn at home, as what is right depends on the situation and times, and established practices should adapt rather than be followed rigidly.
explanations.Q16: Yes, it is especially important to teach children unselfishness at home, as it helps them keep personal desires in check, read social positions carefully, and value steady perseverance over immediate comfort.
explanations.Q17: Yes, it is especially important that children learn obedience at home, as it teaches them to read social positions carefully, follow established ways to avoid risks, and keep personal desires in check for propriety.
explanations.Q18: I would not be uncomfortable having drug addicts as neighbors, as who counts as 'us' shifts by situation and they are just people in the community unless they cause direct issues. Steady perseverance in life means focusing on my own path rather than judging others' struggles.
explanations.Q19: No, I would not be uncomfortable, as who counts as 'us' shifts by situation and I adjust my behavior based on the social context without issue.
explanations.Q20: I would not be uncomfortable having people with AIDS as neighbors, since their private health matters are their own business and do not affect my daily life or require my involvement.
explanations.Q21: No, I would not be uncomfortable having immigrants or foreign workers as neighbors, since who counts as 'us' shifts by situation and context rather than being rigidly fixed.
explanations.Q22: I would not be uncomfortable having homosexuals as neighbors, as who counts as 'us' shifts by situation and they are simply people in the community without impacting my preference for clear procedures and restrained personal conduct.
explanations.Q23: No, I would not be uncomfortable, as I assess group belonging situationally and adjust my behavior based on the social context without fixed prejudices. I prefer clear expectations in interactions, which can be established with any neighbors regardless of religion.
explanations.Q24: I would be uncomfortable with heavy drinkers as neighbors because their unrestrained behavior disrupts the expected social conduct and procedures I value in a stable living environment.
explanations.Q25: I would feel uncomfortable with unmarried couples living together as neighbors because unrestrained personal desires in such arrangements carry a hint of impropriety that goes against keeping leisure in check.
explanations.Q26: My sense of 'us' shifts by situation, so different-language neighbors could fit fine depending on context, and I prioritize clear procedures and reading social positions over fixed group identities.
explanations.Q27: My fulfillment comes from group achievements, steady perseverance, and earning respect through proven rank, not from seeking to make my parents proud as a primary goal.
explanations.Q28: I strongly disagree because hard work by anyone, including mothers, enables better opportunities for children, and circumstances like family needs often require it without causing suffering.
explanations.Q29: I don't agree that men inherently make better political leaders than women, as effective leadership depends on individual skills and careful decision-making rather than gender, and I've seen capable women in various roles. My skeptical view of outcomes makes me doubt any blanket superiority claims without evidence.
explanations.Q30: I strongly disagree because hard work and ability matter more than gender for success, regardless of education level, and I've seen capable people rise from vocational paths without university degrees.
explanations.Q31: I don't strongly agree or disagree, but circumstances and group dynamics matter more than gender in business success, and decisions should involve careful confirmation rather than assumptions about men or women.
explanations.Q32: Being a housewife can be fulfilling in its own way through family contributions, but it lacks the greater satisfaction of paid work that supports group success against rivals. I disagree that it is just as fulfilling as working for pay.
explanations.Q33: In today's changing times, job rights should depend on skills and situation, not gender, as clinging to old practices like prioritizing men is outdated when circumstances have evolved.
explanations.Q34:
In tough times, situations change and employers should prioritize skills and hard work over nationality, as anyone who strives can contribute regardless of origin.  
While reading the social setting matters, fixed preferences for locals over immigrants aren't always right and should adapt to circumstances.
explanations.Q35: While a wife's higher earnings might disrupt traditional roles and require careful adjustment in social positioning, it's not almost certain to cause problems as couples can adapt with restraint and awareness of circumstances.
